paragraphs: Cloud platforms must divide shared computing resources among users whose interests can conflict. Learning a separate resource-management strategy for every interacting user can become difficult as the platform grows. This paper approaches that scaling problem through mean-field games, providing a way to study learning across a large population of competing users.

The authors develop an online natural actor-critic algorithm that accommodates function approximation. This matters because practical serverless platforms have too many possible states and actions to handle by explicitly representing every combination. They prove finite-time convergence to a regularized Nash equilibrium under linear function approximation and softmax parameterization; that theoretical result is specifically tied to those choices.

The implementation is broader than the proof: the authors evaluate both linear and neural-network approximations on OpenWhisk using workloads drawn from production traces. Their experiments report scalability to many users and significant improvements over the evaluated baselines in function latency and resource utilization. The contribution therefore combines a conditional convergence guarantee with practical evidence for managing shared cloud resources.
neurips-2022-a-mean-field-game-approach-.tldr: A mean-field game learning method scales cloud resource management to many users, with conditional convergence guarantees and improved experimental latency and resource efficiency.

paragraphs: Many sign languages have little or no labeled data for learning to recognize signs. This work addresses that shortage by combining learning from unlabeled signing videos with transfer across languages. Its contributions include a pretraining collection, a pretrained recognition model, and multilingual evaluation and training datasets.

SignCorpus contains about 4,600 hours across 10 sign languages. The authors curate internet videos, filter their quality, and convert them into pose-keypoint sequences. They use this collection to pretrain Sign2Vec, a graph-based model with 5.2 million parameters, intended for adaptation to sign-recognition tasks across languages.

The authors also assemble MultiSign-ISLR from 11 labeled datasets spanning seven sign languages, aligning labels across the collection, and introduce MultiSign-FS for fingerspelling across seven languages. Fine-tuning Sign2Vec on these resources produces multilingual isolated-sign recognition models. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show significant gains over state-of-the-art results, supporting the usefulness of both pretraining and multilingual transfer in the evaluated settings. Datasets, models, and code are released through the OpenHands toolkit.
neurips-2022-addressing-resource-scarcit.tldr: Multilingual signing datasets and a pretrained graph model improve sign recognition through self-supervised pretraining and transfer across languages.

paragraphs: Generating an animated face requires both controllable expressions and a coherent appearance as the camera moves. Two-dimensional generators can produce inconsistencies between viewpoints, while existing three-dimensional-aware generators offer limited fine-grained expression control. AniFaceGAN aims to bring these capabilities together in a face-generation model.

Its central design splits the internal three-dimensional representation into two fields. A template field represents identities in a canonical expression, while a deformation field represents how each identity changes expression. This gives expression changes a specific role within the representation, connecting animation control to changes in three-dimensional structure.

During adversarial training, the generator learns to imitate a parametric three-dimensional face model at the three-dimensional level. That supervision helps make the deformation controls correspond to meaningful expressions. Although the training images are unstructured and two-dimensional, the authors report high-quality animatable faces with strong visual consistency across viewpoints. Their experiments show superior performance over prior work, supporting this combination of representation decomposition and imitative training for face animation.
neurips-2022-anifacegan-animatable-3d-aw.tldr: AniFaceGAN separates identity and expression deformation to generate controllable face animations with strong visual consistency across viewpoints.

paragraphs: Keypoints can describe an object's structure for tasks such as animation and image generation, but manually labeling them for each object domain is expensive. AutoLink learns a structural representation from a collection of images of the same object class. Its representation is a graph of two-dimensional points connected by straight edges.

An encoder predicts point locations separately for each image, while a shared latent graph connects the same pairs of points throughout the collection. Both the locations and connection weights are learned. A differentiable edge map combines them, allowing the model to learn through an image-inpainting objective that asks it to reconstruct randomly masked image regions.

The shared connections provide a consistent structure while allowing point positions to change between images. The resulting graphs can be interpretable: on images of people, AutoLink recovers human skeleton topology. The authors report better results than existing self-supervised methods on established keypoint and pose-estimation benchmarks. They also identify the approach as a step toward structure-conditioned generation on more diverse datasets.
neurips-2022-autolink-self-supervised-le.tldr: AutoLink learns interpretable keypoint graphs from unlabeled images by combining shared connections with an image-inpainting objective.

paragraphs: Related time series can provide information about how one another should be aligned. A joint alignment formulation captures this by balancing similarity between aligned signals with agreement between neighboring time-warping functions. Although this can improve alignment, solving its max-flow formulation with general-purpose algorithms requires substantial time and memory.

BILCO is an exact solver designed around the structure of that particular problem. It combines dynamic programming with the push-relabel approach through linear component operations. The motivation is that the joint problem contains many individual dynamic time-warping problems. A second strategy pushes in both directions, using readily computed initial solutions and prior knowledge to reduce unnecessary work.

Across thousands of synthetic datasets and three application categories, BILCO is consistently at least 10 times faster and averages a 20-fold speedup against the best existing max-flow method tested. It uses at most one-eighth as much memory, averaging one-tenth. These findings show that exploiting the alignment problem's structure can make its exact solution substantially more practical.
neurips-2022-bilco-an-efficient-algorith.tldr: BILCO exploits the structure of joint time-series alignment to solve its max-flow problem exactly with substantially less time and memory.

paragraphs: Model Predictive Control repeatedly plans over a finite time window, making its performance sensitive to the information used in each planning problem. This paper develops a general route for bounding dynamic regret, a measure of accumulated performance loss relative to an optimal control benchmark. The central contribution is an analysis pipeline that connects planning sensitivity to overall control performance.

The pipeline starts by deriving a perturbation bound for a finite-time optimal control problem. That bound describes how the solution responds to changes in the problem. The authors then use it to bound the controller's error at each step and, from those stepwise errors, obtain a dynamic-regret bound.

This connection allows established perturbation-analysis tools to support regret analysis in several settings. For linear time-varying systems, the authors extend existing bounds to include prediction errors in costs, dynamics, and disturbances. They also derive bounds for systems with nonlinear dynamics and constraints. Applying the pipeline requires an appropriate perturbation bound, making sensitivity analysis the key entry point.
neurips-2022-bounded-regret-mpc-via-pert.tldr: A perturbation-analysis pipeline bounds Model Predictive Control regret in settings involving prediction errors, nonlinear dynamics, and constraints.

paragraphs: Imitation learning commonly trains a model to map observations directly to an expert's actions. When experts use search, planning, or another multistep algorithm, demonstrations can contain much richer information: the intermediate computations that produced each action. This paper studies how to use those recorded procedures as learning targets.

Procedure cloning treats the expert's full computation sequence as a supervised sequence-prediction problem. The learner imitates intermediate steps as well as the final action. This is particularly relevant when an expert used privileged tools, such as an environment simulator, that the learned agent will not have available when acting. The procedure supplies training information without requiring those tools at inference.

Experiments cover navigation, simulated robotic manipulation, and game playing. The authors report significant generalization to unseen environment configurations, including configurations where directly running the expert procedure is infeasible. These findings support a broader use of demonstrations: learning the recorded path to a decision can help policies transfer beyond the configurations encountered during training.
neurips-2022-chain-of-thought-imitation-.tldr: Procedure cloning learns expert computation sequences alongside actions, improving empirical generalization without requiring the expert's privileged tools at inference.

paragraphs: A useful prediction can depend on a combination of features rather than any single feature alone. In genomics, for example, several mutations might matter together. This paper tackles the discovery of such predictive groups when their membership is not known in advance, extending beyond selecting individual variables or choosing among predefined groups.

The authors define groups through linear and nonlinear interactions between features. Their neural architecture uses an ensemble of feature-selection models to discover those groups directly. The resulting groups are sparse and have minimal overlap, so the representation emphasizes compact combinations without repeatedly selecting largely the same collection of features.

The paper also introduces a metric for comparing discovered groups with known ground-truth groups. Synthetic tasks and semi-synthetic chemistry datasets allow this kind of structural evaluation because the underlying grouping is available. Experiments additionally include an image dataset and a real cancer dataset. Together, these studies demonstrate the method's utility for identifying predictive combinations across several kinds of data.
neurips-2022-composite-feature-selection.tldr: An ensemble of feature-selection models discovers sparse, minimally overlapping predictive feature groups without requiring predefined candidates.

paragraphs: A long planning horizon need not create a large statistical penalty in episodic reinforcement learning, but earlier horizon-free results had important restrictions. They applied either to tabular models or to computationally inefficient algorithms for linear mixture Markov decision processes. This paper provides a computationally efficient horizon-free algorithm for the latter setting.

The method estimates unknown transition dynamics using weighted least squares. Its weights account for both variance and uncertainty, bringing both considerations into the estimation procedure. The resulting regret scales as d times the square root of K, plus d squared, up to logarithmic factors. The authors establish that this rate is optimal up to those factors.

The same estimator also applies to heterogeneous linear bandits. There, the regret bound depends on the square root of the sum of reward variances, multiplied by the context dimension, plus an additional dimension term, again up to logarithmic factors. This improves on the best known algorithms in the stated setting when the reward variances are known.
neurips-2022-computationally-efficient-h.tldr: Variance- and uncertainty-aware estimation enables computationally efficient horizon-free learning with near-optimal regret for linear mixture MDPs.

paragraphs: Deciding whether an action causes harm requires more than observing its outcome: it can require comparing that outcome with what would have happened under another action. This paper formalizes harm and benefit using causal models, making counterfactual comparisons part of the decision-making objective.

The authors show that definitions based only on factual outcomes fail to identify harmful actions in certain scenarios. They also establish a result in which standard learning algorithms lacking counterfactual reasoning are guaranteed to pursue harmful policies following distribution shifts. These findings motivate a framework that explicitly optimizes counterfactual objectives to make decisions averse to harm.

The framework is demonstrated through drug-dose selection using a dose-response model learned from randomized trial data. In that analysis, selecting doses through standard treatment-effect methods produces unnecessarily harmful choices. The counterfactual approach identifies significantly less harmful doses without sacrificing efficacy. The example illustrates how evaluating benefit and harm through causal alternatives can change a decision even when maintaining treatment effectiveness remains a goal.
neurips-2022-counterfactual-harm-83fa144.tldr: A causal definition of harm supports counterfactual decision objectives that identify less harmful drug doses without reduced efficacy in the paper's demonstration.

paragraphs: Video object segmentation needs to carry useful information from previous frames into the current one. In the AOT approach, hierarchical propagation gradually turns general visual features into features associated with particular objects. The paper identifies a cost of this transformation: deeper propagation loses object-independent visual information as object-specific information grows.

DeAOT separates these two types of information into independent propagation branches. One handles general visual embeddings, while the other handles object-specific embeddings. To compensate for the extra computation of using two branches, the authors introduce a Gated Propagation Module built with single-head attention.

Experiments show significant improvements over AOT in both accuracy and efficiency. On YouTube-VOS, reported operating points include 86.0% at 22.4 frames per second and 82.0% at 53.4 frames per second. The authors also report state-of-the-art results on YouTube-VOS, DAVIS 2017, DAVIS 2016, and VOT 2020 without test-time augmentation. These results support preserving general appearance information alongside object identity throughout hierarchical propagation.
neurips-2022-decoupling-features-in-hier.tldr: DeAOT separates general visual and object-specific feature propagation, improving video segmentation accuracy and efficiency over AOT.

paragraphs: Change-point detection asks whether a sequence has changed and where that change occurred. This paper studies paired observations consisting of a target and associated covariates. Its focus is a change in the target's distribution conditional on those covariates, extending the usual analysis of changes in a variable's marginal distribution.

The authors build their methodology in stages. They first study changes in conditional expectation, which concerns the target's average value given the covariates. They then generalize the tools developed for that simpler task to conditional distributions, allowing the analysis to address more than changes in the conditional average.

The paper derives large-sample properties of its proposed statistics and evaluates the method against baselines adapted from existing tools. Two real-data applications further demonstrate its potential. The contribution brings together a method for this paired-data problem and an analysis of its statistical behavior. Its emphasis on conditioning makes the relationship between the target and its covariates central to identifying a change.
neurips-2022-detection-and-localization-.tldr: The paper develops statistically analyzed methods for detecting and locating changes in a target's distribution conditional on its covariates.

paragraphs: Interactive assignments such as games and websites can engage students, but evaluating them requires examining how they behave during interaction. Manual grading is costly, and a simple correct-or-incorrect verdict gives students little guidance about their mistakes. This paper develops an automated approach that seeks specific errors by interacting with a student's program.

The authors formulate error discovery as a meta-exploration problem. This provides an objective for deciding how to explore programs and an algorithm for optimizing that objective. The aim is to reach states that reveal particular mistakes, allowing the system to give finer-grained feedback than a binary assessment.

Evaluation uses more than 700,000 real anonymized submissions from one Code.org interactive assignment. The method achieves 94.3% feedback accuracy, with a reported improvement of 17.7% over existing approaches and performance within 1.5% of human-level accuracy. These results show that learning how to explore program behavior can support detailed automated feedback in the studied assignment, addressing an important obstacle to grading interactive work at scale.
neurips-2022-giving-feedback-on-interact.tldr: A meta-exploration agent interacts with student programs to discover specific errors, achieving 94.3% feedback accuracy on a large Code.org assignment dataset.

paragraphs: GLIPv2 brings object localization and image-language understanding into one model. Localization includes finding objects or identifying their individual image regions; understanding includes answering questions about images and generating captions. The paper's goal is to make training for these activities support a common set of model weights.

The approach combines three pretraining tasks. Phrase grounding expresses object detection through links between language phrases and image regions. Region-word contrastive learning trains relationships between visual regions and words. Masked language modeling adds a task of recovering hidden language content. Together, these objectives unify localization pretraining with vision-language pretraining and simplify an earlier multistage procedure.

Experiments show that the shared model reaches near-state-of-the-art performance across several localization and understanding tasks. The authors also report strong zero-shot and few-shot adaptation for open-vocabulary object detection, alongside superior grounding on vision-language understanding tasks. These findings support the claim that the two task families can benefit each other, with one model learning both where described content appears and how visual content relates to language.
neurips-2022-glipv2-unifying-localizatio.tldr: GLIPv2 unifies localization and vision-language pretraining in one shared model, achieving near-state-of-the-art results across both task families.

paragraphs: An explanation can be evaluated by whether it helps someone predict a model's behavior on new examples. This paper makes that teaching goal part of how explanations are learned. It focuses on students learning to simulate a teacher model, with success measured on examples where explanations are no longer provided.

Using meta-learning, the authors optimize explanations so that student models become better at reproducing the teacher's decisions. The explanation is therefore judged through its effect on subsequent learning. This creates a direct connection between the stated purpose of an explanation and the training objective used to produce it.

Across three tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, students trained with the learned explanations simulate the teacher significantly more effectively than students using explanations from previous methods. Human annotations and a user study additionally find closer alignment with how people would explain the required decisions. The results support teaching effectiveness as a practical objective for explanation design, with evidence from both student-model behavior and human judgments.
neurips-2022-learning-to-scaffold-optimi.tldr: Meta-learning produces explanations that better teach student models to simulate a teacher and more closely match human explanations in the evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Neural-network guidance has helped traditional search solve difficult planning instances, but understanding that success requires examining how the guidance affects exploration. This paper studies best-first search for Sokoban, focusing on the interaction between policy and value networks. It finds that the policy network is a surprisingly effective search heuristic, with further benefits from the value network.

The authors examine search-cost distributions and find that Sokoban instances can have heavy tails on both sides of their runtime distributions. They report the existence of left heavy tails and propose an abstract tree model that empirically explains their appearance. This connects the observed runtime behavior to the structure of the search.

Experiments indicate that policy guidance can avoid exploring exponentially large subtrees, producing left heavy tails with polynomial scaling. That finding concerns the studied search behavior, rather than establishing polynomial complexity for Sokoban generally. The results also emphasize random restarts as an important tool for handling both left and right heavy tails in neural-network-guided search.
neurips-2022-left-heavy-tails-and-the-ef.tldr: Sokoban experiments link effective policy-network search guidance to heavy-tailed runtimes and highlight the value of random restarts.

paragraphs: A classifier's predicted label does not by itself explain how uncertain that prediction is. This paper proposes a fast, scalable way to quantify prediction uncertainty for a single deterministic neural network. Its starting point is a nonparametric estimate of the distribution of labels conditional on a data representation.

The method uses the Nadaraya-Watson estimator and operates directly in feature space. For a neural network, that space can be the embedding the network assigns to its inputs. The authors show how to use the estimated conditional label distribution to explicitly separate aleatoric uncertainty from epistemic uncertainty, distinguishing uncertainty associated with the data from uncertainty associated with knowledge of the prediction.

The authors evaluate the approach on text-classification tasks and image datasets including MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-100, and several ImageNet versions. They report strong performance on uncertainty-estimation tasks. The contribution is a feature-space route to uncertainty measurement that can be applied through a network's induced embeddings while retaining an explicit distinction between the two uncertainty types.
neurips-2022-nonparametric-uncertainty-q.tldr: A nonparametric estimator measures and separates aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty using the feature embeddings of a single deterministic network.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the distribution a model is meant to handle. Many approaches using training outlier exposure rely on softmax-derived or energy scores. This paper investigates an alternative probabilistic formulation through a latent-variable model called Conditional-i.

Conditional-i draws on independent component analysis and uses the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion to optimize dependencies between variables. It specifically encodes useful class-conditioning information within the probabilistic model. That construction provides a basis for theoretical analysis of the detection task, connecting the model's dependency structure to its detection objective.

The authors introduce memory-bank architectures to make end-to-end training feasible within a tractable computational budget. Benchmark experiments show a clear performance improvement over state-of-the-art methods in the reported evaluation. The paper also supplies theoretical justification that its training strategy bounds detection error. Together, the architecture and analysis offer an alternative to commonly used detection scores, with empirical gains and an error-bound result supporting the proposed training strategy.
neurips-2022-out-of-distribution-detecti.tldr: Conditional-i uses a class-conditioned latent-variable model and kernel independence criterion for out-of-distribution detection, with benchmark gains and theoretical error bounds.

paragraphs: Multilingual training can help launch unsupervised translation for languages with limited resources. However, the same mixture that supplies useful initial knowledge may later impede improvement because its languages differ. This paper examines how a low-resource translation task can retain the benefit of multilingual pretraining while receiving more focused refinement.

The proposed procedure separates languages from a pretrained multilingual unsupervised translation model so that it concentrates on the target low-resource task. The approach treats multilingual training as a useful starting point and task-focused refinement as a subsequent stage. Its motivation is that continued joint treatment of different languages may hinder further progress on the target translation problem.

The method achieves state-of-the-art results on fully unsupervised translation from English into Nepali, Sinhala, Gujarati, Latvian, Estonian, and Kazakh. Reported BLEU gains are 3.5, 3.5, 3.3, 4.1, 4.2, and 3.3, respectively. These findings support separating the benefits of broad multilingual initialization from the needs of later specialization in the evaluated low-resource translation tasks.
neurips-2022-refining-low-resource-unsup.tldr: Separating target languages from a pretrained multilingual model improves fully unsupervised English translation into six low-resource languages.

paragraphs: Optimizing average reward can leave a reinforcement-learning objective insensitive to outcomes in the tails of the reward distribution. In settings motivated by healthcare or robotics, those outcomes may deserve explicit attention. This paper studies learning objectives that account for risk, including Conditional Value at Risk, commonly called CVaR.

The main contribution is a set of regret bounds for a general class of risk-sensitive objectives. Regret measures the performance lost while learning relative to the relevant optimal benchmark. The authors identify these as the first such bounds for their class, extending theoretical performance analysis beyond an objective based solely on expected reward.

The theory rests on a new characterization of CVaR and a new construction of an optimistic Markov decision process. These provide the ingredients for analyzing learning under the risk-sensitive objective. The result offers a mathematical account of learning performance when tail outcomes matter. Its contribution is the regret theory itself, with healthcare and robotics serving as motivations for the objective.
neurips-2022-regret-bounds-for-risk-sens.tldr: The paper proves regret bounds for a general class of risk-sensitive reinforcement-learning objectives, including CVaR.

paragraphs: Video super-resolution combines information across frames to improve image detail. Models commonly align neighboring frames before combining them, but this paper questions how that practice interacts with transformer attention. Experiments show that transformers can use information from unaligned frames and that existing alignment methods can sometimes hurt their performance.

Removing alignment and expanding the attention window can improve results, but the authors identify two problems with that design: computation rises sharply, and it cannot handle large motions. Their proposed patch alignment method addresses these issues by aligning image patches rather than individual pixels.

Transformers equipped with patch alignment demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks. The findings do not imply that alignment is universally unnecessary; they show that its usefulness depends on how the network gathers information across frames. Patch alignment offers an efficient alternative suited to the studied transformer setting, while the broader analysis helps explain why alignment choices should account for the network and dataset.
neurips-2022-rethinking-alignment-in-vid.tldr: Experiments challenge pixel-level alignment in video super-resolution transformers and motivate efficient patch alignment with state-of-the-art benchmark results.

paragraphs: In decentralized optimization, the communication network and its associated weight matrix influence how quickly distributed learning can converge. Existing results had established an optimal rate for certain linear-graph weight matrices, leaving the general case unclear. This paper establishes optimal convergence rates for smooth, nonconvex stochastic decentralized optimization with general weight matrices.

The authors also analyze losses satisfying the additional Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition and establish an optimal rate for that setting. The extra condition defines a distinct case within the analysis; its result should therefore be read separately from the broader nonconvex result. Both address the performance limits imposed by decentralized communication.

The proof approach uses a Ring-Lattice graph to accommodate general weight matrices while preserving the needed relationship between graph diameter and matrix connectivity. The authors explain that existing lines of analysis do not obtain these results. They then develop a decentralized algorithm attaining both optimal rates up to logarithmic factors, connecting the theoretical limits to an algorithm that nearly reaches them.
neurips-2022-revisiting-optimal-converge.tldr: The paper establishes optimal decentralized nonconvex convergence rates for general weight matrices and an algorithm achieving them up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: The effect of network size on robustness depends on more than whether a model is wide or deep. This paper studies average robustness in selected combinations of width, depth, initialization, and training regime. Its theoretical results identify cases where changing the same architectural property has opposite effects.

For width, the authors prove a negative effect in the under-parameterized setting and an improvement in the over-parameterized setting. Depth interacts closely with initialization and training mode. Under lazy training with LeCun initialization, greater depth helps robustness. With Neural Tangent Kernel or He initialization, the reported effect of depth is harmful.

The paper also examines non-lazy training and demonstrates how increasing width benefits robustness in a two-layer ReLU network. Taken together, the results make parameterization, initialization, and training regime essential parts of any interpretation of architecture and robustness. The conclusions apply to the analyzed settings and average-robustness notion, providing a more conditional account than a blanket recommendation to increase width or depth.
neurips-2022-robustness-in-deep-learning.tldr: Theory shows that width and depth can help or hurt average robustness depending on parameterization, initialization, and training regime.

paragraphs: Video, audio, and text recorded at the same time need not describe the same content. A speaker may discuss something absent from the current image. This paper studies how such semantic mismatches can make cross-modal alignment a noisy training signal and potentially hinder scaling to larger, more varied datasets.

The authors observe strong conflicts between gradients from different alignment losses within individual video-audio-text triplets in VATT pretraining. They propose two responses. Gradient realignment modifies the loss gradients so their directions agree more closely. A gradient-based curriculum uses conflict as an indicator of sample noisiness and prioritizes less noisy triplets during training.

Applying these techniques to VATT pretraining on HowTo100M consistently improves performance on different downstream tasks. The authors also scale training to the more complicated, non-narrative YouTube8M dataset and report further state-of-the-art improvements. These experiments support using training-gradient disagreement to manage imperfect cross-modal supervision, while the broader motivation concerns the difficulty of treating temporal correspondence as reliable semantic correspondence.
neurips-2022-scaling-multimodal-pre-trai.tldr: Realigning conflicting gradients and prioritizing less noisy samples improves multimodal pretraining and supports scaling to more heterogeneous videos.

paragraphs: Backdoor behavior can arise from poisoned training data, but it can also emerge during otherwise benign training. This paper addresses both injected and natural backdoors. It argues that defenses relying on differences in training behavior can be bypassed by slow poisoning and do not cover natural backdoors.

The authors identify a geometric distinction: backdoor-related neurons form a hyperplane classification surface across the input domains of affected labels. Their analysis connects this surface to piecewise-linear functions. They introduce NONE, a training method designed to prevent the formation of these hyperplanes and thereby remove injected backdoors.

Experiments cover five datasets, five state-of-the-art attacks, and benign training. The authors report that NONE can outperform existing state-of-the-art defenses. On average, attack success rates are lower than those of undefended models by factors of 54.83 for standard poisoning attacks and 1.75 for natural backdoors. The results support targeting the identified classification geometry during training, with substantially different reported reduction factors for the two types of backdoor behavior.
neurips-2022-training-with-more-confiden.tldr: NONE modifies training to suppress hyperplane structures associated with backdoors, reducing injected and natural backdoor attack success in experiments.
